title: Virtual memory
relevance: SDE interviews use virtual memory to test whether candidates understand how processes run with limited RAM via demand paging, TLBs, replacement, and thrashing.

phases.goal: Establish what virtual memory and demand paging are, and that page faults are the normal mechanism.

must_hit.point: Virtual memory lets a process execute without being entirely in physical memory by keeping actively used pages in RAM and the rest on a disk backing store (swap), giving each process the illusion of a large contiguous address space larger than physical memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions swap/backing store and the illusion of a larger contiguous address space than RAM.

must_hit.point: Demand paging brings a page into a frame only when it is first referenced, never in advance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States pages are loaded on first reference, not prefetched by the demand-paging design.

must_hit.point: Each page-table entry has a valid/invalid bit: valid means the page is in a frame; invalid means it is on disk or illegal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Correctly maps valid→in frame and invalid→on disk or illegal.

must_hit.point: A page fault is a normal, expected trap that makes demand paging work, not an error—but disk involvement makes the fault rate dominate performance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls page faults expected/normal and ties cost to disk I/O and fault rate.

probes: What is virtual memory, and how does demand paging use the valid/invalid bit?
Is a page fault an error? What actually happens when one occurs?

hints.1: Think about how a process can run when not all of its pages are in RAM.
hints.2: Connect demand paging to the page-table valid/invalid bit and the trap on an invalid reference.
hints.3: Virtual memory keeps hot pages in RAM and the rest on swap; a page is brought in only on first reference; invalid PTE → page fault, which is expected, not a bug.

phases.goal: Walk through the page-fault path, EMAT, the TLB, and how replacement chooses a victim.

must_hit.point: On a page fault the OS checks the reference is legal, finds or frees a frame, schedules a disk read, marks the PTE valid, and restarts the faulting instruction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists legality check, frame allocation/replacement, disk read, PTE update, and instruction restart.

must_hit.point: Effective memory access time with fault rate p, memory access m, and fault service cost s is EMAT = (1−p)·m + p·s; because s is roughly a hundred thousand times m, even a tiny fault rate inflates EMAT sharply.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the EMAT formula and that disk-scale s vs memory-scale m makes low p critical.

must_hit.point: A naive page-table walk costs two memory accesses per reference; a TLB caches recent page→frame translations so a hit yields the frame immediately and a miss falls back to the page table then loads the TLB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions the two-access cost without a TLB and hit vs miss behavior.

must_hit.point: With TLB access c, memory access m, and hit ratio h: EMAT = h(c+m) + (1−h)(c+2m); for c = 10 ns, m = 50 ns, h = 0.8, EMAT = 70 ns.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the TLB EMAT formula and/or the worked 10/50/0.8 → 70 ns result.

must_hit.point: When no free frame exists, the OS evicts a victim and writes it back only if its dirty bit is set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links eviction to the dirty bit and write-back only when dirty.

probes: Walk through what the OS does on a page fault, step by step.
Why do we need a TLB, and how does it change effective memory access time?
When a victim page is replaced, when must it be written back to disk?

hints.1: Start from an invalid PTE and list the OS steps before the instruction can retry.
hints.2: Separate pure demand-paging EMAT (p, m, s) from the TLB formula (h, c, m) and mention dirty-bit write-back.
hints.3: Fault path: legality → free/replace frame → disk read → valid PTE → restart; EMAT=(1−p)m+ps; TLB avoids two memory accesses; write back only if dirty.

phases.goal: Compare replacement policies on the shared reference string and identify Belady's anomaly.

must_hit.point: On the 15-reference string with three frames, Optimal gets 8 faults and 7 hits; FIFO and LRU each get 12 faults and 3 hits; MRU is worst with 13 faults and 2 hits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls the fault/hit counts for OPT/FIFO/LRU/MRU on that trace.

must_hit.point: FIFO can exhibit Belady's anomaly: for 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 it has 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames—more frames made it worse.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States Belady's anomaly under FIFO with the 9-vs-10 fault example.

must_hit.point: Optimal evicts the page unused furthest in the future and is unrealizable in practice but is the yardstick; LRU approximates it from the past and, like Optimal, never exhibits Belady's anomaly (unlike FIFO, which is not a stack algorithm).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts OPT (future, ideal), LRU (past, no Belady), and FIFO (can Belady).

must_hit.point: MRU is rarely a good general policy but can help for patterns like a large file scanned once, where the most-recently-used page is least likely to be needed again.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives when MRU helps (sequential once-through) vs general poor performance.

probes: Compare FIFO, Optimal, LRU, and MRU on the standard three-frame reference string.
What is Belady's anomaly, and which algorithms can / cannot show it?
When might you prefer MRU over LRU?

hints.1: Recall which policy looks at age in memory, past use, future use, or most-recent use.
hints.2: Use the three-frame fault counts and the FIFO Belady example with 3 vs 4 frames.
hints.3: OPT 8/7, FIFO&LRU 12/3, MRU 13/2; FIFO can Belady (9→10 faults); LRU/OPT never; MRU for scan-once patterns.

phases.goal: Apply virtual memory ideas to thrashing control and common OS optimizations.

must_hit.point: Thrashing is when a process or system spends more time servicing page faults than doing useful work; as multiprogramming rises, CPU utilization climbs, peaks, then collapses sharply.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines thrashing and describes the utilization climb-peak-collapse shape.

must_hit.point: The working-set model tracks pages referenced in a recent window and gives a process enough frames for that set; admit new processes only if working sets fit, otherwise reduce multiprogramming by swapping a process out.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains working-set sizing and reducing degree of multiprogramming when demand exceeds frames.

must_hit.point: Copy-on-write after fork shares read-only physical frames until a write, then copies that single page.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes shared RO pages until write triggers a private copy.

must_hit.point: mmap maps a file into the address space so access is ordinary demand-paged memory and can be shared; the page cache keeps recently used disk pages in otherwise-free RAM with lazy write-back of dirty pages.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links mmap to demand-paged file access/sharing and free RAM as a disk page cache.

probes: What is thrashing, and how does the working-set model address it?
How does copy-on-write speed up fork?
What are memory-mapped files and the page cache doing in terms of virtual memory?

hints.1: Picture too many processes each with too few frames for their active pages.
hints.2: Remedy with working sets and lower multiprogramming; then connect fork COW and mmap/page cache.
hints.3: Thrashing = paging dominates work; give each process its working set or swap one out; COW shares until write; mmap/page cache demand-page and cache disk in free RAM.

tradeoffs.topic: FIFO vs Optimal vs LRU vs MRU
tradeoffs.strong_answer: On the shared 15-reference, three-frame string: Optimal 8 faults / 7 hits (best, needs future knowledge); FIFO and LRU both 12 / 3; MRU worst at 13 / 2. LRU approximates Optimal from the past and avoids Belady's anomaly; FIFO is simple but can Belady; MRU only for special patterns like a once-through file scan.

tradeoffs.topic: More frames vs fewer faults (Belady's anomaly)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Intuition says more frames mean fewer faults, but FIFO can violate that: on 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 it has 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. Belady's anomaly hits non-stack algorithms like FIFO; LRU and Optimal never show it.

tradeoffs.topic: Keeping fault rate low vs raw memory speed
tradeoffs.strong_answer: EMAT = (1−p)m + p·s; because fault service s is roughly a hundred thousand times memory access m, a tiny p dominates—so good replacement and enough frames matter more than raw m alone.

gotchas.trap: Treating a page fault as an error or rare failure.
gotchas.correction: A page fault is a normal, expected trap—the mechanism that makes demand paging work; the danger is a high fault rate, not the fault itself.

gotchas.trap: Assuming more frames always reduce page faults under every replacement policy.
gotchas.correction: Under FIFO, Belady's anomaly can make more frames worse (9 faults with 3 frames vs 10 with 4 on the classic string); LRU and Optimal do not exhibit this.

gotchas.trap: Thinking Optimal page replacement is a practical online policy.
gotchas.correction: Optimal needs future references, so it is unrealizable in practice; it is only the yardstick; LRU approximates it from the past.

gotchas.trap: Always writing a victim page back to disk on eviction.
gotchas.correction: Write back only if the dirty bit is set; a clean victim can be discarded.

gotchas.trap: Responding to thrashing by raising the degree of multiprogramming further.
gotchas.correction: Thrashing means too few frames per active working set; use the working-set model and reduce multiprogramming (swap a process out) when demand exceeds available frames.
